activities.mastery_criterion: Students correctly round 4 out of 5 numbers to the specified decimal places.
activities.task: Students receive a set of raw calculator outputs from division problems (e.g., 10/3 = 3.333333). They practice applying the three rounding rules to round these numbers to one and two decimal places, explaining which rule they used for each.

activities.mastery_criterion: Students correctly match all cards and write at least two valid original examples of scientific notation.
activities.task: Students play a matching game where they pair cards showing standard large/small numbers (e.g., distance to the sun, size of a cell) with their corresponding scientific notation cards. They then write three of their own examples.

activities.mastery_criterion: Students correctly identify the precision and accuracy of the target hits and provide a logical justification based on the definitions.
activities.task: Students throw wet paper balls at a drawn target on the board. They analyze the grouping of the hits to determine if the throws were precise (grouped together), accurate (near the center), both, or neither, and write a short justification.

activities.mastery_criterion: Students correctly categorize the error in 3 out of 4 case studies and provide a plausible prevention method.
activities.task: Students read a series of short case studies describing failed scientific experiments or measurements. They must highlight the source of the error, categorize it as personal, instrumental, or environmental, and propose a way to prevent it.

activities.mastery_criterion: Students correctly calculate the area and apply the error propagation formula to find the final uncertainty.
activities.task: Students measure the dimensions of their textbook using a ruler, noting the instrument's minimum division as the error. They calculate the area of the book cover and apply the taught formula to find the propagated error of the area.

activities.mastery_criterion: Students score 80% or higher on the rubric, demonstrating accurate identification, comparison, and reasoning regarding mechanical energy.
activities.task: Students complete a written assessment analyzing diagrams of mechanical systems (springs, ramps, pendulums), comparing energy states, and justifying energy transformations.

activities.mastery_criterion: Students score 80% or higher on the rubric, demonstrating accurate application and reasoning across all kinematics and dynamics micros.
activities.task: Students complete a written assessment featuring scenario-based questions requiring them to calculate displacement, read map coordinates, classify motion types from data tables, predict motion from force diagrams, and justify torque applications.

context_tasks.protected-areas: Students connect their social studies knowledge of El Salvador's departments with geographic coordinates. They are given a list of departments and must find their approximate center coordinates on a map.

activities.mastery_criterion: Students accurately determine the latitude and longitude for at least 3 departments.
activities.task: Students connect their social studies knowledge of the supplied location's departments with geographic coordinates. They are given a list of departments and must find their approximate center coordinates on a map.

activities.mastery_criterion: Accurate plotting of points and correct calculation showing displacement is zero for a closed loop.
activities.task: Students review Cartesian coordinate graphing from math class. They plot a series of points to form a shape, then calculate the distance of the perimeter and the displacement from the first point to the last point (which should be zero if closed).

activities.mastery_criterion: Accurate measurement of both path distance and straight-line displacement, clearly distinguishing the two in their presentation.
activities.task: Students design an obstacle course on a grid drawn on the playground. They map a path through the obstacles, measure the total distance of the path, and then measure the direct displacement from start to finish. They present their map and measurements to the class.

activities.mastery_criterion: Students correctly apply the definition of MCU to evaluate their own experimental setup, noting variations in rotation speed.
activities.task: Students build a simple centrifuge using a salad spinner. They place a small marked object inside, spin it at a steady rate, and attempt to count rotations per 10 seconds. They analyze the difficulty of maintaining constant angular speed and write a report on whether their manual spinning truly achieved MCU.

activities.mastery_criterion: Students produce a linear graph and correctly argue that the constant slope indicates constant speed, fulfilling MRU criteria.
activities.task: Students set up a tall clear bottle filled with oil. They drop a small bead into the oil and use a stopwatch to time its descent past evenly spaced marks on the bottle. They graph position vs. time and use the straight-line graph to justify classifying the motion as MRU.

activities.mastery_criterion: Students correctly isolate variables, showing that greater height (more potential energy) and greater mass (more kinetic energy) both result in the cup sliding further.
activities.task: Students roll marbles of different masses down a ramp from different heights into a plastic cup. They measure how far the cup slides. They conduct trials varying only height (to test gravitational potential) and then varying only mass (to test kinetic energy impact). They write a report comparing the effects.

activities.mastery_criterion: Students correctly identify that greater stretch (deformation) stores more elastic potential energy, evidenced by the longer launch distance.
activities.task: Students build a simple rubber band launcher using cardboard tubes. They measure how far a paper ball is launched when the rubber band is pulled back 2 cm, 4 cm, and 6 cm. They record the data and write a summary identifying how the stretch distance relates to the stored elastic potential energy.

activities.mastery_criterion: Students collect accurate force data showing less force is needed further from the hinge, and justify this using the concept of lever arm and torque.
activities.task: Students use a spring scale to pull open a heavy door from three different measured distances from the hinge. They record the force required at each distance. They graph Force vs. Distance from Hinge and write a conclusion justifying the inverse relationship based on torque requirements.

activities.mastery_criterion: Students accurately measure and sum the path segments for distance and correctly measure the straight-line displacement, explaining the difference.
activities.task: Students work in groups to map out a multi-leg journey across the school courtyard. They use measuring tapes to record the distance of each leg and sum them up for the total distance. Finally, they measure the straight-line displacement from the start to the end point and compare the two values.

activities.mastery_criterion: Students correctly identify that all deformed elastic objects store energy and rank them qualitatively based on stiffness and stretch.
activities.task: Students test different elastic materials (various rubber bands, soft springs) by stretching them to different lengths and observing the force required. They categorize the materials based on how much elastic potential energy they seem to store when deformed.

activities.mastery_criterion: Accurate justification of energy states at all 4 points, clearly describing the continuous transformation between potential and kinetic energy.
activities.task: Students analyze a diagram of a roller coaster track with 4 labeled points. They must write a paragraph for each point, justifying the relative amounts of potential and kinetic energy based on the height and expected speed, and explaining the transformations between points.

activities.mastery_criterion: Accurate calculation of net force and correct prediction of motion state based on Newton's First Law.
activities.task: Students are given a worksheet with 5 diagrams of objects with various force vectors applied. They must calculate the net force for each. If the net force is zero, they predict the object's motion state (rest or constant velocity) and justify it.

context_tasks.seismic-risk: Students use a detailed map of El Salvador to locate specific volcanoes and national parks given their latitude and longitude coordinates. They record the name of the feature found at each coordinate.

activities.mastery_criterion: Students correctly identify at least 4 out of 5 geographical features based on the provided coordinates.
activities.task: Students use a detailed map of the supplied location to locate specific volcanoes and national parks given their latitude and longitude coordinates. They record the name of the feature found at each coordinate.

activities.mastery_criterion: Correct identification of at least 4 out of 5 locations based on the coordinates.
activities.task: Students receive a list of 5 geographic coordinates. They must locate each on a provided map, identify the geographical feature or city at that location, and record it in a table.

activities.mastery_criterion: Accurate drawing of the path and correct calculation of both distance and displacement.
activities.task: Students are given a blank grid and a starting point. The teacher reads a sequence of movements. Students draw the path, calculate total distance, and draw/measure the displacement vector. They compare answers with a partner.

activities.mastery_criterion: Correct identification of the longest distance and displacement, with a clear explanation distinguishing path length from straight-line change.
activities.task: Students analyze three pre-drawn paths on a grid. They must identify which path has the longest distance, which has the longest displacement, and write a sentence explaining why the two answers are different.

activities.mastery_criterion: Accurate justification of energy transformation, noting max potential at the edges and max kinetic at the bottom.
activities.task: Students watch a short video of a skateboarder in a half-pipe. They sketch the half-pipe, mark three positions, and write a brief justification of how potential and kinetic energy transform as the skater moves back and forth.

activities.mastery_criterion: Correct sequencing of cards and accurate description of energy transformations at each stage.
activities.task: Students are given a set of cards showing different stages of a bouncing ball. They must sequence the cards and write a sentence for each transition explaining the energy transformation occurring (e.g., falling: potential to kinetic; hitting ground: kinetic to elastic potential).

activities.mastery_criterion: Accurate net force calculation and correct prediction of the motion state.
activities.task: Students receive a quick quiz with 3 force diagrams. They must calculate the net force for each and predict if the object will remain at rest/constant velocity or accelerate.

activities.mastery_criterion: Correct classification of MRU and MCU with accurate reference to trajectory and constant speed/rotation.
activities.task: Students are shown 4 short video clips of different motions (a car on a straight highway, a spinning fan, a bouncing ball, a pendulum). They must quickly classify each as MRU, MCU, or neither, and write one sentence justifying their choice.

activities.mastery_criterion: Students correctly calculate the period of rotation and justify the MCU classification using the circular trajectory and constant rotation rate.
activities.task: Students observe a marked spinning object (like a bicycle wheel or a top). They use a stopwatch to time how long it takes for the mark to complete 5 full rotations, then calculate the time per rotation. They write a paragraph classifying the motion as MCU, citing the circular path and constant time per rotation.

activities.mastery_criterion: Students correctly calculate equal distances for equal time intervals and explicitly state both MRU conditions (straight line, constant speed).
activities.task: Students analyze a video or simulation of a car moving along a straight track. They record the car's position every 2 seconds in a data table. They calculate the distance covered in each interval, observe that it is constant, and write a statement classifying the motion as MRU based on the straight path and constant speed.

activities.mastery_criterion: Students correctly record a larger value for distance than displacement and define distance as the path taken and displacement as the straight-line change in position.
activities.task: Students walk a specific path marked on the classroom floor (e.g., 3 steps forward, 4 steps right). They measure the total path length with a measuring tape (distance) and then measure the straight line from start to finish (displacement). They record both values and write a definition for each based on their physical experience.

activities.mastery_criterion: Students correctly identify only the stretched/compressed objects as having elastic potential energy and illustrate the deformation.
activities.task: Students examine various objects: a relaxed rubber band, a stretched rubber band, an uncompressed spring, and a compressed spring. They categorize which objects currently store elastic potential energy and draw diagrams showing the deformation that causes the stored energy.

activities.mastery_criterion: Students correctly label max potential at the top, max kinetic at the bottom, and justify the continuous transformation between height and speed.
activities.task: Students build a simple pendulum with string and a washer. They release it and observe the swing. They draw the pendulum at three positions: highest point, lowest point, and opposite highest point. They label where potential energy is max/min and where kinetic energy is max/min, and write a paragraph justifying how energy transforms between the two forms during the swing.

activities.mastery_criterion: Students accurately place dots at the correct intersections of latitude and longitude for all 3 given coordinates.
activities.task: Students receive a map with a latitude and longitude grid. The teacher models finding a specific coordinate. Students then practice finding 3 specific coordinates provided by the teacher, marking them with a dot, and writing the name of the feature located there.

activities.mastery_criterion: Students record deeper craters for greater heights and conclude that higher elevation means greater gravitational potential energy.
activities.task: Students drop a small ball into a container of sand from three different heights (0.5m, 1m, 1.5m). They measure the depth of the crater formed each time as an indicator of energy. They record the data and write a conclusion comparing the gravitational potential energy at the different heights.

activities.mastery_criterion: Students measure a greater push distance for the faster car and conclude that higher speed results in greater kinetic energy.
activities.task: Students roll a toy car down a ramp into a lightweight block. They do this from a low release point (slow speed at bottom) and a high release point (fast speed at bottom). They measure how far the block is pushed each time. They write a statement comparing the kinetic energy of the car at the two different speeds.

activities.mastery_criterion: Students correctly draw canceling force arrows and predict either rest or constant velocity, citing zero net force.
activities.task: Students analyze scenarios presented on cards (e.g., a book resting on a table, a hockey puck gliding on frictionless ice). For each, they draw force arrows (gravity, normal force, applied force, friction). If forces cancel out (net force zero), they predict the resulting motion (rest or constant velocity) and justify their reasoning in writing.

activities.mastery_criterion: Students correctly identify the handle position as requiring the least force and justify this by referencing the longer lever arm distance from the axis of rotation.
activities.task: Students push a classroom door closed using one finger at three different points: near the hinge, in the middle, and near the handle. They rank the points by how much effort was required. They then draw a diagram of the door, labeling the axis of rotation and the lever arm distances, and write a justification for why the handle position is most effective.

activities.mastery_criterion: Both level counts and the total match the supplied record.
activities.task: Complete the task independently using a new diagram and then justify the response. A model record assigns 2 electrons to level 1 and 6 to level 2. Place eight counters accordingly and check the total. Do not derive an orbital configuration.

activities.mastery_criterion: Both level counts and the total match the supplied record.
activities.task: Compare two fresh teacher-provided records and correct one deliberately flawed representation. A model record assigns 2 electrons to level 1 and 6 to level 2. Place eight counters accordingly and check the total. Do not derive an orbital configuration.

activities.mastery_criterion: Both level counts and the total match the supplied record.
activities.task: Teacher models one worked example, students explain the representation in pairs, then complete an independent check. A model record assigns 2 electrons to level 1 and 6 to level 2. Place eight counters accordingly and check the total. Do not derive an orbital configuration.

activities.mastery_criterion: Students score 1 point for predicting the correct interaction and 1 point for citing the rule of charges.
activities.task: Students complete a written quiz with 3 scenarios describing charged objects. They must predict the interaction (attract/repel) and explain why.

activities.mastery_criterion: Students predict repulsion and explain that both balloons acquired the same negative charge.
activities.task: Students read a scenario about two balloons rubbed with wool. They must predict what happens when the balloons are brought together and write an explanation based on their charges.

activities.mastery_criterion: Students correctly draw arrows pointing towards each other for opposites and away for likes, with correct written justifications.
activities.task: Students are given diagrams of various charged particles (e.g., two cations, one cation and one anion). They must draw arrows to predict the direction of movement (attraction or repulsion) and justify it.

activities.mastery_criterion: Students can state the rule that like charges repel and opposite charges attract.
activities.task: Introduce the concept of electrostatic interactions. Explain that like charges repel and opposite charges attract. Demonstrate using a theoretical model on the board.

activities.mastery_criterion: Students score 1 point for correct classification and 1 point for a justification based on electron loss/gain.
activities.task: Students are given 4 atomic scenarios with proton and electron counts. They must classify each as a cation or anion and write a one-sentence justification.

activities.mastery_criterion: Students correctly sort the cards and justify their choices based on comparing proton and electron counts.
activities.task: Students receive cards with scenarios (e.g., 'Atom has 11 protons and 10 electrons'). They must sort the cards into 'Cation', 'Anion', or 'Neutral' bins and write a justification for each.

activities.mastery_criterion: Students can define cation and anion in terms of electron loss or gain.
activities.task: Explain how atoms become ions by losing or gaining electrons. Define cations (positive, lost electrons) and anions (negative, gained electrons). Show examples on the board.

activities.mastery_criterion: Students score 1 point for identifying them as the same element/isotopes and 1 point for justifying based on equal protons and unequal neutrons.
activities.task: Students are given a scenario: 'Atom X has 6 protons and 6 neutrons. Atom Y has 6 protons and 8 neutrons.' They must state if they are the same element and justify their answer in writing.

activities.mastery_criterion: Students correctly identify the isotope pairs and justify their answers based on proton counts.
activities.task: Students are given a list of 10 pairs of atoms with their proton and neutron counts. They must analyze each pair and determine if they are isotopes of the same element or different elements.

activities.mastery_criterion: Students group the correct models together as isotopes and explain that they have the same number of proton tokens.
activities.task: Students use colored tokens to build the nuclei of different atoms based on given data. They must visually compare their models to determine which ones represent isotopes of the same element.

activities.mastery_criterion: Students can define isotopes based on equal protons and unequal neutrons.
activities.task: Define isotopes as atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons. Show examples on the board comparing proton and neutron counts of Carbon-12 and Carbon-14.

activities.mastery_criterion: Students score 1 point for correctly labeling the nucleus and 1 point for correctly placing protons/neutrons inside and electrons outside.
activities.task: Students complete a blank diagram of an atom under test conditions, labeling the nucleus, protons, neutrons, and electrons without using notes.

activities.mastery_criterion: Students construct a model with a central nucleus containing protons and neutrons, and electrons on the outside, correctly labeled.
activities.task: Students use playdough of three different colors to build a 3D model of an atom. They use toothpicks and paper flags to label the nucleus, protons, neutrons, and electrons.

activities.mastery_criterion: Students correctly identify and label the subatomic particles across at least three different visual representations of atoms.
activities.task: Provide students with various printed diagrams of different atomic models (e.g., Bohr, Rutherford). Students must identify and label the subatomic particles in each different representation.

activities.mastery_criterion: Students produce a recognizable sketch with all four key terms correctly placed.
activities.task: Students use personal whiteboards to quickly sketch an atom and label its parts from memory as a warm-up activity.

activities.mastery_criterion: Students correctly label the nucleus, protons, neutrons, and electrons in their notebook diagrams.
activities.task: Introduce the atomic model by drawing a large diagram on the board. Explain the nucleus, protons, neutrons, and electrons. Students copy the diagram into their notebooks and label each part using colored pencils.

activities.mastery_criterion: Students score 1 point for setting up the correct subtraction and 1 point for the correct final answer for each question.
activities.task: Students take a quiz where they must calculate the number of neutrons for 5 specific elements, showing their subtraction work.

activities.mastery_criterion: Students correctly calculate the number of neutrons for at least 12 out of 15 elements.
activities.task: Students complete a worksheet containing 15 different elements with given mass numbers and atomic numbers, calculating the neutrons for each.

activities.mastery_criterion: Students correctly calculate neutrons and state that isotopes of the same element have different numbers of neutrons.
activities.task: Students are given data cards for different isotopes of carbon and oxygen. They must calculate the neutrons for each and identify patterns in how the mass number changes.

activities.mastery_criterion: Students can articulate the formula: Neutrons = Mass Number - Atomic Number.
activities.task: Explain the concepts of mass number and atomic number. Demonstrate how to subtract the atomic number from the mass number to find the number of neutrons using examples on the board.

activities.mastery_criterion: Rejects the claim and cites the fixed-orbit limitation rather than treating either drawing as a photograph.
activities.task: Complete the task independently using a new diagram and then justify the response. Compare a circle diagram and an electron-cloud diagram. A character claims the drawn circle proves the electron follows that exact path. Use the supplied model note to accept or reject the claim.

activities.mastery_criterion: Rejects the claim and cites the fixed-orbit limitation rather than treating either drawing as a photograph.
activities.task: Compare two fresh teacher-provided records and correct one deliberately flawed representation. Compare a circle diagram and an electron-cloud diagram. A character claims the drawn circle proves the electron follows that exact path. Use the supplied model note to accept or reject the claim.

activities.mastery_criterion: Rejects the claim and cites the fixed-orbit limitation rather than treating either drawing as a photograph.
activities.task: Compare two fresh teacher-provided records and correct one deliberately flawed representation. Compare a circle diagram and an electron-cloud diagram. A character claims the drawn circle proves the electron follows that exact path. Use the supplied model note to accept or reject the claim.

activities.mastery_criterion: Correctly reads every marked level and identifies the representation as a model.
activities.task: Complete the task independently using a new diagram and then justify the response. Given a diagram with levels numbered 1, 2 and 3, identify the level occupied by each marked electron. State that the diagram is a representation, not a photograph.

activities.mastery_criterion: Correctly reads every marked level and identifies the representation as a model.
activities.task: Compare two fresh teacher-provided records and correct one deliberately flawed representation. Given a diagram with levels numbered 1, 2 and 3, identify the level occupied by each marked electron. State that the diagram is a representation, not a photograph.

activities.mastery_criterion: Correctly reads every marked level and identifies the representation as a model.
activities.task: Compare two fresh teacher-provided records and correct one deliberately flawed representation. Given a diagram with levels numbered 1, 2 and 3, identify the level occupied by each marked electron. State that the diagram is a representation, not a photograph.

activities.mastery_criterion: Correctly reads every marked level and identifies the representation as a model.
activities.task: After a delay, reconstruct the principle from memory and apply it to a fresh labelled diagram. Given a diagram with levels numbered 1, 2 and 3, identify the level occupied by each marked electron. State that the diagram is a representation, not a photograph.

activities.mastery_criterion: Correctly reads every marked level and identifies the representation as a model.
activities.task: After a delay, reconstruct the principle from memory and apply it to a fresh labelled diagram. Given a diagram with levels numbered 1, 2 and 3, identify the level occupied by each marked electron. State that the diagram is a representation, not a photograph.

activities.mastery_criterion: Justifies the direction of the average using the relative counts.
activities.task: Use ten counters representing a hypothetical mixture of lighter and heavier isotopes. Compare a nine-to-one mixture with a one-to-nine mixture and explain which average lies closer to the lighter mass. Do not calculate percentage-weighted formulas.

activities.mastery_criterion: Justifies the direction of the average using the relative counts.
activities.task: Use ten counters representing a hypothetical mixture of lighter and heavier isotopes. Compare a nine-to-one mixture with a one-to-nine mixture and explain which average lies closer to the lighter mass. Do not calculate percentage-weighted formulas.

activities.mastery_criterion: 1 point for each correct match.
activities.task: Compare a teacher-worked representation with one incorrect example, identify the governing observation or counting rule, then complete an individual check. Match the scientist to their proposed atomic model.

activities.mastery_criterion: Rejects the claim and cites the fixed-orbit limitation rather than treating either drawing as a photograph.
activities.task: Compare a teacher-worked representation with one incorrect example, identify the governing observation or counting rule, then complete an individual check. Compare a circle diagram and an electron-cloud diagram. A character claims the drawn circle proves the electron follows that exact path. Use the supplied model note to accept or reject the claim.

activities.mastery_criterion: Correctly reads every marked level and identifies the representation as a model.
activities.task: Compare a teacher-worked representation with one incorrect example, identify the governing observation or counting rule, then complete an individual check. Given a diagram with levels numbered 1, 2 and 3, identify the level occupied by each marked electron. State that the diagram is a representation, not a photograph.

activities.mastery_criterion: Correctly identifies donor and receiver and conserves the total in the supplied diagram.
activities.task: Compare a teacher-worked representation with one incorrect example, identify the governing observation or counting rule, then complete an individual check. A supplied diagram shows one electron counter moving from atom A to atom B. Record which atom loses and which gains an electron and check that the total electron count is unchanged.

activities.mastery_criterion: Student selects the correct element and justifies it mentioning the trend across a period.
activities.task: Given a pair of elements in the same period (e.g., Potassium and Bromine), students predict which has a larger atomic radius and write a justification explaining why based on nuclear charge.

activities.mastery_criterion: Student correctly identifies the number of protons and electrons for all three elements.
activities.task: Given the atomic numbers of three elements, students state the number of protons and electrons for each neutral atom.

activities.mastery_criterion: Student correctly lists both elements and their exact atom counts for all formulas.
activities.task: Students are given a list of five chemical formulas and must write down the names of the elements present and the exact number of atoms for each element in the formula.

activities.mastery_criterion: Student correctly colors Group 1 (excluding Hydrogen) and labels it 'alkali metals'.
activities.task: Students are given a blank periodic table and must color Group 1 (excluding Hydrogen) and label it with the accurate family name 'alkali metals'.

activities.mastery_criterion: Student correctly writes all five chemical formulas, simplifying subscripts correctly.
activities.task: Students are given five pairs of cations and anions with their oxidation numbers. They must construct the correct chemical formula for each pair, ensuring subscripts are simplified where appropriate.

activities.mastery_criterion: Reads the two supplied outer-electron patterns and identifies their common group from the provided table.
activities.task: Compare supplied level diagrams for lithium and sodium using an explicit key for the outermost energy level. Count the outer electrons and check the provided periodic table. Do not derive orbital configurations or generalize the rule to every element.

activities.mastery_criterion: Student correctly matches all three models and provides an accurate basic description for each.
activities.task: Students match the names of Döbereiner, Chancourtois, and Newlands with their respective classification models (triads, helix, octaves) and write a one-sentence description of each.

activities.mastery_criterion: Student correctly classifies all three examples.
activities.task: Students read three short descriptions of atoms gaining or losing electrons and classify each as forming a cation or an anion.

activities.mastery_criterion: Correctly compares the supplied records and limits the conclusion to the evidence shown.
activities.task: Compare two supplied, explicitly illustrative pairs of neutral-atom and positive-ion radius records. Identify the pattern in those pairs, then explain why those records alone do not prove an unrestricted rule for all comparisons.

activities.mastery_criterion: Student places all five element symbols in the exact correct cells based on coordinates.
activities.task: Given a blank periodic table grid and a list of five group and period coordinates, students must write the correct element symbols in the corresponding cells.

activities.mastery_criterion: Student correctly assigns the oxidation number for all four elements.
activities.task: Given a list of four elements from groups 1, 2, 16, and 17, students determine the typical oxidation number for each.

activities.mastery_criterion: Student correctly orders the physical models and uses them to explain the trend across a period and down a group.
activities.task: Students use concentric paper circles to physically model the atomic radius of elements in Period 3 and Group 1. They arrange the models to show the trends and use their physical models to explain why the radius changes.

activities.mastery_criterion: Student correctly determines the number of subatomic particles for at least 4 out of 5 given elements.
activities.task: Students practice identifying the number of protons, neutrons, and electrons for various elements using their atomic numbers.

context_tasks.protected-areas: Using examples from Salvadoran contexts like salt processing, students build physical models of NaCl, KCl, and KI using modeling clay. They then list the elements and exact atom counts for each formula based on their models.

activities.mastery_criterion: Student correctly lists the elements and exact atom counts matching their physical models.
activities.task: Using examples from the supplied location contexts like salt processing, students build physical models of NaCl, KCl, and KI using modeling clay. They then list the elements and exact atom counts for each formula based on their models.

activities.mastery_criterion: Student correctly sorts all given elements into their respective family bins.
activities.task: Students receive a list of elements and must sort them into three labeled bins (Alkali Metals, Halogens, Noble Gases) based on their group number on the periodic table. They then record their sorted lists on a worksheet.

activities.mastery_criterion: Student correctly constructs and writes the simplified chemical formulas for the puzzle pairs.
activities.task: Students use puzzle pieces representing cations and anions with their respective oxidation numbers. They must physically match the pieces to balance the charges, then write the resulting chemical formula on their worksheet, simplifying subscripts when needed.

activities.mastery_criterion: Reads the two supplied outer-electron patterns and identifies their common group from the provided table.
activities.task: Compare supplied level diagrams for lithium and sodium using an explicit key for the outermost energy level. Count the outer electrons and check the provided periodic table. Do not derive orbital configurations or generalize the rule to every element.

activities.mastery_criterion: Student correctly identifies the ion type and charge for at least 4 out of 5 scenarios.
activities.task: Students are given a list of scenarios where atoms gain or lose specific numbers of electrons. They must determine if the resulting ion is a cation or an anion and write its overall charge.

activities.mastery_criterion: Correctly compares the supplied records and limits the conclusion to the evidence shown.
activities.task: Compare two supplied, explicitly illustrative pairs of neutral-atom and positive-ion radius records. Identify the pattern in those pairs, then explain why those records alone do not prove an unrestricted rule for all comparisons.

activities.mastery_criterion: Student correctly writes the element symbol in the exact cell corresponding to the given group and period.
activities.task: Students play a coordinate mapping game in pairs. One student calls out a group and period number, and the other must identify the element symbol at that intersection on their blank periodic table grid, writing it in the correct cell.

activities.mastery_criterion: Student correctly determines the oxidation number for all listed elements based on their groups.
activities.task: Students receive a list of elements and must determine their typical oxidation number by finding their group on the periodic table. They record the element, its group, and its oxidation number in a table.

activities.mastery_criterion: Student correctly places the three models in chronological order and accurately explains the logic of each.
activities.task: Students create a timeline of the periodic table's development. They place Döbereiner, Chancourtois, and Newlands on the timeline, draw their models, and write a brief explanation of the logic behind each classification system.

context_tasks.protected-areas: Students research and create a presentation on the industrial applications of specific elements (e.g., copper in wiring, aluminum in construction), connecting them to everyday uses in El Salvador.

activities.mastery_criterion: Student identifies at least two elements and accurately describes their industrial applications in a local context.
activities.task: Students research and create a presentation on the industrial applications of specific elements (e.g., copper in wiring, aluminum in construction), connecting them to everyday uses in the supplied location.

activities.mastery_criterion: Student correctly lists elements and atom counts for all three formulas.
activities.task: Students complete a 'do-now' mini-quiz on the board where they break down three common chemical formulas into their constituent elements and atom counts.

activities.mastery_criterion: Student correctly identifies the larger atom and references the group or period trend.
activities.task: Students participate in a quick flashcard game where they are shown pairs of elements and must quickly point to the one with the larger atomic radius, explaining the trend.

activities.mastery_criterion: Student correctly identifies the decreasing trend of atomic radius across a period.
activities.task: Demonstrate the trend of atomic radius across a period. Use a visual model showing how increased nuclear charge pulls the electron cloud closer, decreasing the radius from left to right. Students annotate a periodic table with arrows showing the trend.

activities.mastery_criterion: Student correctly identifies the location and charge of protons, neutrons, and electrons.
activities.task: Introduce the basic structure of an atom, including protons, neutrons, and electrons. Demonstrate how to determine the number of each subatomic particle using the atomic number.

activities.mastery_criterion: Student correctly lists the elements and their respective atom counts from a given formula.
activities.task: Explain how to read a chemical formula, focusing on the meaning of subscripts. Demonstrate with H2O, showing that the subscript 2 applies to Hydrogen and the absence of a subscript means one Oxygen atom. Students practice with three simple formulas on the board.

activities.mastery_criterion: Student correctly identifies the family name for a given group of elements.
activities.task: Explain the concept of element families sharing similar properties. Identify and color-code the alkali metals, halogens, and noble gases on a demonstration periodic table. Students follow along on their own charts.

activities.mastery_criterion: Student correctly writes a chemical formula by crossing charges and simplifying if necessary.
activities.task: Demonstrate how to construct a chemical formula by crossing the oxidation numbers of a cation and an anion. Show examples where subscripts are simplified (e.g., Ca+2 and O-2 becoming CaO). Students practice three guided examples.

activities.mastery_criterion: Reads the two supplied outer-electron patterns and identifies their common group from the provided table.
activities.task: Compare supplied level diagrams for lithium and sodium using an explicit key for the outermost energy level. Count the outer electrons and check the provided periodic table. Do not derive orbital configurations or generalize the rule to every element.

activities.mastery_criterion: Student correctly matches the name of the historical model with its visual representation.
activities.task: Present the historical progression of element classification using visual diagrams of Dobereiner triads, Chancourtois telluric helix, and Newlands octaves. Students observe the diagrams and trace the patterns described by each scientist using colored markers on printed handouts.

activities.mastery_criterion: Student correctly identifies the resulting ion type when an atom gains or loses electrons.
activities.task: Define cations and anions. Explain that losing electrons results in a positive charge (cation) and gaining electrons results in a negative charge (anion). Use a balance scale analogy to show protons vs electrons. Students practice identifying the ion type for three examples.

activities.mastery_criterion: Correctly compares the supplied records and limits the conclusion to the evidence shown.
activities.task: Compare two supplied, explicitly illustrative pairs of neutral-atom and positive-ion radius records. Identify the pattern in those pairs, then explain why those records alone do not prove an unrestricted rule for all comparisons.

activities.mastery_criterion: Student accurately finds the symbol of an element given its group and period coordinates.
activities.task: Introduce the modern periodic table layout, defining groups as vertical columns and periods as horizontal rows. Demonstrate how to find an element using its group and period coordinates, similar to a map grid. Students practice finding three guided examples.

activities.mastery_criterion: Student correctly assigns the typical oxidation number to an element based on its group.
activities.task: Introduce the concept of oxidation numbers as the charge an atom contributes. Show how representative elements in groups 1, 2, and 13-17 have typical oxidation numbers based on their group. Students label a blank periodic table with these common oxidation numbers.

activities.mastery_criterion: Student correctly identifies nebulae, main sequence stars, red giants, and white dwarfs from descriptions.
activities.task: Students complete a written quiz where they are given four descriptions of stellar characteristics and must write the correct stage name next to each description without a word bank.

activities.mastery_criterion: Student explains that the crust formed from the cooling of a magma ocean.
activities.task: Students are given a prompt asking them to explain how the Earth's crust formed according to the terrestrial model. They must write a brief summary without using their notes.

activities.mastery_criterion: Student diagram includes and correctly labels all four required components, with a valid justification for their specific design choices.
activities.task: Students are given a specific mission context (e.g., monitoring weather patterns over the ocean). They must design a satellite for this mission, drawing a diagram and justifying their choice of scientific instruments, power source, container, and communication system based on the mission's novel context.

activities.mastery_criterion: Student correctly matches all three vehicles to their functional descriptions in the mission scenarios.
activities.task: Students complete a multiple-choice and short-answer quiz where they are given descriptions of missions (e.g., 'We need to monitor weather patterns from orbit without a crew') and must identify which vehicle (space station, satellite, or rover) is required.

activities.mastery_criterion: Student connects the absence of the magnetosphere to the destructive impact of solar wind on habitability.
activities.task: Students answer a constructed-response question: 'Explain what would happen to Earth's habitability if the magnetosphere suddenly disappeared. Use evidence about solar wind in your answer.'

activities.mastery_criterion: Student links the red shift to the stretching of wavelengths and the object moving away in a clear written response.
activities.task: Students read a scenario about a newly discovered galaxy whose light spectrum is heavily shifted toward the red end. They must write a formal scientific response determining the direction of its movement relative to Earth and justifying their answer using the concept of wavelength stretching.

activities.mastery_criterion: Student correctly identifies the crust, mantle, outer core, and inner core in the correct order.
activities.task: Students complete a diagram labeling quiz where they must write the names of the four main layers of the Earth in the correct boxes pointing to a cross-section image.

activities.mastery_criterion: Student correctly aligns mass with the final stage and references mass as the determining factor in their essay.
activities.task: Students are presented with a short text describing two newly observed stars nearing the end of their lives, one very massive and one similar to our Sun. They must write a short essay predicting their final stages and explaining why their paths diverge.

activities.mastery_criterion: Student correctly orders the stages from dust particles to a full planet and matches them to their descriptions.
activities.task: Students complete a matching and sequencing worksheet where they must draw lines connecting the terms (dust, chondrules, meteoroids, asteroids, planetesimals, planets) to their definitions, and then write them in a numbered list from smallest/earliest to largest/latest.

activities.mastery_criterion: Student correctly plots the new coordinates (doubling the distance from the origin) and states that all points moved away from each other.
activities.task: Students are given a worksheet with a diagram of a grid representing space with galaxies at specific coordinates. They must draw a second grid showing the universe expanded by a factor of two, placing the galaxies at their new coordinates and writing a short explanation of the model.

activities.mastery_criterion: Student successfully identifies the missing/incorrect components and produces a corrected diagram with all four required parts labeled.
activities.task: Students are given a 'flawed' blueprint of a satellite that is missing key components or has them incorrectly labeled. They must identify the errors, redraw the blueprint correctly, and ensure the container, power source, scientific instruments, and communication system are all present and properly labeled.

activities.mastery_criterion: Student correctly orders the four layers from exterior to interior and accurately identifies their states of matter.
activities.task: Students construct a 2D foldable model of the Earth using concentric paper circles of decreasing sizes. They must label each layer (crust, mantle, outer core, inner core) and write its state of matter (solid or liquid) underneath the flap.

activities.mastery_criterion: Student accurately records the distances and explains that points further away move a greater distance, modeling expansion.
activities.task: Students use a large rubber band with evenly spaced dots to model expansion. They stretch the band along a ruler, record the new positions of the dots, and calculate the proportional increase in distance to reinforce the concept of universal expansion.

activities.mastery_criterion: Student correctly sequences all six stages of accretion and provides accurate visual representations for each.
activities.task: Students create a six-panel comic strip illustrating the accretion process. They must draw and label each stage (dust, chondrules, meteoroids, asteroids, planetesimals, planets) in the correct chronological order.

activities.mastery_criterion: Student correctly matches at least 3 out of 4 stages to their descriptions and visuals.
activities.task: Students play a matching game where they must pair a card with a visual representation of a star stage to a card with its text description. Once all pairs are found, they glue them into their notebooks and write one additional fact for each stage.

activities.mastery_criterion: Student's summary mentions the cooling of magma or internal processes forming the solid layer.
activities.task: Students read a short text about the terrestrial model of crust formation. They must highlight key terms (magma, cooling, solid, crust) and then write a 5-sentence summary explaining the process in their own words, imagining they are explaining it to a younger sibling.

context_tasks.seismic-risk: Students read a brief informational text about El Salvador's volcanic chain (e.g., the Apaneca-Ilamatepec range). They then draw a detailed blueprint of a satellite designed to monitor this volcanic activity. They must label the container, solar panels (power), infrared cameras (instruments), and antenna (communication), and write a sentence for each explaining its specific role in this mission.

activities.mastery_criterion: Student creates a diagram with all required satellite components labeled and explained in the context of the mission.
activities.task: Students read a brief informational text about the supplied location's volcanic chain (e.g., the Apaneca-Ilamatepec range). They then draw a detailed blueprint of a satellite designed to monitor this volcanic activity. They must label the container, solar panels (power), infrared cameras (instruments), and antenna (communication), and write a sentence for each explaining its specific role in this mission.

activities.mastery_criterion: Student correctly identifies the functions and characteristics of space stations, satellites, and rovers in their brochure.
activities.task: Students create a foldable brochure with three sections: Space Station, Satellite, and Rover. In each section, they must draw a simple icon, write its primary function, and list whether it carries humans, orbits a body, or lands on a surface.

activities.mastery_criterion: Student connects the absence of the magnetosphere to the destructive impact of solar wind on habitability, using evidence.
activities.task: Students analyze a case study of Mars, which lost its magnetosphere. They read data about Mars' current atmosphere and surface radiation levels. They must write a comparative paragraph justifying what would happen to Earth's habitability if its magnetosphere disappeared, using the Mars data as evidence.

activities.mastery_criterion: Student accurately sorts the galaxies and links the red shift to the stretching of wavelengths and the object moving away.
activities.task: Students are given a set of cards with data from different galaxies, including their observed spectral lines compared to laboratory standards. They must sort the galaxies into 'moving away', 'moving closer', or 'stationary', and write a paragraph justifying their sorting based on the stretching or compressing of the light waves.

activities.mastery_criterion: Student correctly labels all four layers in the correct order from exterior to interior.
activities.task: Students are given a large blank diagram of the Earth's cross-section. They must color each layer, draw a line to a text box, and write the name of the layer along with one key fact (e.g., composition or state of matter) sourced from their textbook.

activities.mastery_criterion: Student correctly categorizes the stars based on mass and articulates that high mass leads to supernovae and low mass to white dwarfs.
activities.task: Students are given a list of ten hypothetical stars with their masses listed in solar masses. They must create a T-chart predicting whether each star will end as a white dwarf or undergo a supernova, and write a summary paragraph explaining the rule they used to make their predictions.

activities.mastery_criterion: Student correctly orders the stages from dust particles to a full planet on their timeline.
activities.task: Students work in small groups with a set of 20 cards containing images and descriptions of accretion stages. They must race to arrange them in the correct chronological order of formation, then create a timeline poster gluing the cards in sequence.

activities.mastery_criterion: Student accurately graphs the positions showing that marks further away move a greater distance than marks closer to the origin.
activities.task: Students use a large elastic band with evenly spaced marks to model expansion along a single line of sight between galaxies. One student holds the end while another stretches it along a meter stick. They record the positions of the marks at rest, at 50cm stretch, and at 100cm stretch, graphing the movement of each mark relative to the starting point.

activities.mastery_criterion: Student illustrates and explains that the loss of the magnetic field allows solar wind to reach the surface, destroying habitability.
activities.task: Students are given a 'What If?' scenario card stating the Earth's core has completely solidified, stopping the magnetic field. They have 15 minutes to sketch a before-and-after picture of Earth's surface and write a brief caption explaining the change in habitability.

activities.mastery_criterion: Student correctly identifies the stretched wave as redshift and explains it indicates movement away from the observer.
activities.task: Students participate in a quick-write activity where they are shown a single image of a stretched wave and a compressed wave. They must identify which represents redshift and explain why this means a galaxy is moving away from Earth.

activities.mastery_criterion: Student articulates that the magnetosphere blocks solar wind/radiation, and leaving it removes that protection.
activities.task: Students participate in a 'Think-Pair-Share' where they must verbally justify to a partner why astronauts traveling to Mars face higher radiation risks than those on the International Space Station (which is within Earth's magnetosphere). They then write down their partner's best point.

activities.mastery_criterion: Student correctly identifies false statements and rewrites them to accurately reflect that redshift means wavelengths are stretching as objects move away.
activities.task: Students are given a true/false quiz with statements about light waves and galaxy movement. For every false statement, they must rewrite it to make it true, specifically focusing on the relationship between redshift and expansion.

activities.mastery_criterion: Student correctly identifies nebulae, main sequence stars, red giants, and white dwarfs based on their characteristics.
activities.task: Students are given a set of 'stellar profile' folders containing characteristics (temperature, size, composition) of different star stages. They work in groups to categorize the profiles into nebula, main sequence, red giant, and white dwarf, using a reference text to verify their classifications.

activities.mastery_criterion: Student explains that the crust formed from the cooling and solidifying of a magma ocean in their storyboard.
activities.task: Students mix cornstarch and water to create a thick paste representing magma. They spread it in a shallow dish and observe as it dries and forms a solid crust on top, drawing a storyboard with three panels showing the wet mixture, the drying process, and the final solid crust, writing a descriptive caption for each.

activities.mastery_criterion: Student creates a functional model with all required satellite components included and identifiable.
activities.task: Students act as aerospace engineers. They are given a list of required satellite components (container, power source, scientific instruments, communication system). They use craft materials to build a 3D prototype of a satellite, ensuring all four components are present and identifiable, then present their model to the class.

activities.mastery_criterion: Student correctly identifies the purpose of different space exploration vehicles and matches them to their descriptions.
activities.task: Students examine large posters of a space station, a satellite, and a rover. They work in groups to list the visible features of each (e.g., wheels, solar panels, living quarters). They then match functional descriptions provided by the teacher to the correct vehicle based on their feature lists.

activities.mastery_criterion: Student argues that without the magnetosphere, solar wind would make Earth uninhabitable, connecting the shield concept to habitability.
activities.task: Students place a bar magnet inside a plastic bag and sprinkle iron filings on top to visualize a magnetic field. The teacher uses a fan (solar wind) to blow lightweight particles (confetti) at the bag, showing how a physical barrier deflects them. Students then write an argument explaining why Earth's magnetic field is necessary for life, using the demonstration as an analogy.

activities.mastery_criterion: Student correctly identifies that a shift toward longer wavelengths indicates an object is moving away and justifies this using the wave model.
activities.task: Students use a coiled spring toy (slinky) to model light waves. They stretch the spring while moving one end away from a stationary observer to simulate how wavelengths lengthen (redshift). They then review three hypothetical star spectrum charts and justify which stars are moving away based on the shift of absorption lines toward the red end.

activities.mastery_criterion: Student correctly identifies and labels the crust, mantle, outer core, and inner core in the correct order.
activities.task: Students build a cross-section model of the Earth using four different colors of modeling dough. They cut the sphere in half to reveal the layers and use toothpicks with paper flags to label the crust, mantle, outer core, and inner core.

activities.mastery_criterion: Student deduces that high-mass stars become supernovae/black holes while low-mass stars become white dwarfs, referencing mass as the determining factor.
activities.task: Students analyze a flowchart showing the life cycles of stars based on initial mass. They are given two case studies: Star A (0.8 solar masses) and Star B (25 solar masses). They must trace the path of each star on the flowchart and write a justification for their final evolutionary stages based on the mass data.

activities.mastery_criterion: Student correctly orders and models the stages from dust particles to a full planet.
activities.task: Students use different sizes of modeling clay to represent the stages of accretion. They start with tiny specks (dust), combine them into small balls (chondrules), then larger lumps (meteoroids/asteroids), and finally a large sphere (planet). They label each stage on a large piece of paper.

activities.mastery_criterion: Student successfully creates a model showing proportional expansion between points and records accurate measurements.
activities.task: Students work in pairs to draw dots on a deflated balloon, measure the distances between them with a flexible tape, inflate the balloon halfway, measure again, and then inflate fully and measure a final time. They record the data in a table and write a conclusion about how the distance between all points increases simultaneously.

activities.mastery_criterion: Correctly identifies both terms and provides a justification based on energy versus surface effects.
activities.task: Read two short reports: one detailing the energy released at the epicenter and another describing the structural damage in a city. Identify which report describes magnitude and which describes intensity, justifying the choice.

activities.mastery_criterion: Correctly predicts the bare soil will erode more and justifies it by referencing the stabilizing effect of vegetation.
activities.task: Predict which of two inclined soil trays (one bare, one covered with grass) will lose more soil when equal amounts of water are poured over them, and justify the choice using evidence of root stabilization.

activities.mastery_criterion: All four stages must be placed in the exact chronological sequence.
activities.task: Arrange four descriptions of an organism dying, being buried, compacting into rock, and being exposed in the correct chronological order on the assessment sheet.

activities.mastery_criterion: Correctly categorizes all provided land descriptions to their appropriate use capacity.
activities.task: Match descriptions of land plots (e.g., flat fertile plains vs. steep rocky hillsides) to their ideal potential use categories (e.g., intensive agriculture vs. forest conservation).

activities.mastery_criterion: Correctly points out the extinction events and the Cambrian explosion.
activities.task: Identify the periods of mass extinctions and the Cambrian explosion on a provided geological time scale.

activities.mastery_criterion: Correctly classifies all three boundary types based on the directional arrows.
activities.task: Given three diagrams showing arrows of plate movement (moving apart, colliding, sliding past), classify each as convergent, divergent, or transform.

activities.mastery_criterion: Correctly sequences all layers in the provided diagram from bottom (oldest) to top (youngest).
activities.task: Given a diagram of sedimentary rock layers with embedded fossils, sequence the layers from oldest to youngest on the provided assessment sheet.

activities.mastery_criterion: Correctly matches all provided descriptions to the corresponding layers in the diagram.
activities.task: Label a diagram of a soil profile with the correct horizons based on provided descriptions of color, organic matter, and rock content.

activities.mastery_criterion: Provides the correct mathematical calculation and final percentage.
activities.task: Given the total volume of a settled soil sample in a jar and the volume of its sand layer, calculate the percentage of sand in the sample.

activities.mastery_criterion: Selects only seismic activity and gas emissions without including unrelated environmental factors.
activities.task: Select the correct volcanic monitoring parameters from a mixed multiple-choice list that includes seismic activity, wind speed, gas emissions, and lunar phases.

activities.mastery_criterion: Correctly highlights energy descriptions in yellow and damage descriptions in pink, with a logical written justification.
activities.task: Students read excerpts from historical hazard reports. They use a yellow highlighter for sentences describing energy released (magnitude) and a pink highlighter for sentences describing structural damage (intensity). They write a sentence justifying one of their choices.

activities.mastery_criterion: The experimental design includes a control (bare soil) and variables, with a logical hypothesis referencing root or cover stabilization.
activities.task: Students design an experiment on paper to test different types of ground cover (e.g., leaves, twigs, planted seeds) against erosion. They must write a hypothesis predicting which cover will be most effective and justify it based on the concept of soil stabilization.

activities.mastery_criterion: All description cards are glued in the exact chronological sequence: death, burial, compaction, exposure.
activities.task: Students receive a set of mixed description cards detailing the fossilization process. They must sort the cards into the correct chronological timeline and glue them onto a timeline poster.

activities.mastery_criterion: All profile cards are sorted into the correct use category based on their physical descriptions.
activities.task: Students sort profile cards of different land plots (describing slope, soil depth, and rockiness) into ideal use categories (intensive agriculture, pasture, forest conservation).

activities.mastery_criterion: All event cards are placed in the correct geological periods.
activities.task: Students are given a blank geological time scale and a set of event cards (mass extinctions, Cambrian explosion). They must place the events in the correct periods on the timeline.

activities.mastery_criterion: All boundaries on the map are correctly color-coded according to the directional arrows.
activities.task: Students analyze abstract maps showing tectonic plates with directional arrows. They must color-code the boundaries (e.g., red for convergent, blue for divergent, green for transform) based on the arrows.

activities.mastery_criterion: Students correctly sequence the layers and explicitly mention that lower layers were deposited before upper layers.
activities.task: Students analyze paper diagrams of sedimentary rock layers containing different shapes representing fossils. They must sequence the layers from oldest to youngest and write a short paragraph explaining their reasoning based on the principle of superposition.

activities.mastery_criterion: The diagram is colored to match the descriptions (e.g., dark top, rocky bottom) and correctly labeled with horizon names.
activities.task: Students receive a blank cross-sectional diagram of soil and a text describing the color, organic matter, and rock content of three horizons. They must color the diagram accordingly and label each horizon.

activities.mastery_criterion: Accurately measures the layers in millimeters and correctly calculates the sand percentage using the formula.
activities.task: Students work in groups with pre-settled plastic jars of different soil samples. They use rulers to measure the total soil height and the sand layer height, then calculate the percentage of sand for their specific jar.

activities.mastery_criterion: Students successfully filter the log, circling only seismic and gas data while crossing out weather data.
activities.task: Students review a mock data log from an observatory. The log contains mixed data (seismic tremors, gas levels, rainfall, wind direction). Students must cross out the irrelevant data and circle the parameters that indicate volcanic activity.

activities.mastery_criterion: Report A contains only energy-related facts; Report B contains only surface-effect descriptions.
activities.task: Students write two short fictional news reports about the same earthquake. Report A must focus strictly on the magnitude (seismograph readings, energy). Report B must focus strictly on the intensity (how people felt it, damage to buildings).

activities.mastery_criterion: Correctly identifies deforested areas as high risk and justifies the prediction by explaining the lack of root stabilization.
activities.task: Students analyze photographs of different hillsides (some forested, some deforested). They must predict which areas are at highest risk for erosion during a heavy rainstorm and write a paragraph justifying their predictions using evidence of vegetation cover.

activities.mastery_criterion: The comic strip accurately depicts and describes death, burial, compaction, and exposure in order.
activities.task: Students create a four-panel comic strip illustrating the stages of fossilization for a fictional organism. They must include captions for each panel describing the specific stage.

activities.mastery_criterion: The map correctly assigns agriculture to flat/fertile areas and forestry to steep/rocky areas.
activities.task: Students create a land-use map for a fictional town. They are given a base map with topographical lines and soil descriptions. They must color-code areas for agriculture, forestry, and urban development based on the land's capacity.

activities.mastery_criterion: Students successfully assemble all three-piece puzzles correctly matching name, arrows, and feature.
activities.task: Students complete a matching puzzle activity where they connect three pieces: the boundary name, a diagram of the arrows, and a simple drawing of the resulting geological feature (e.g., trench, ridge).

activities.mastery_criterion: The collage is correctly labeled with the bottom-most layer identified as the oldest and the top-most as the youngest.
activities.task: Students create a 2D paper collage representing a geological cross-section. They cut out different textured papers to represent rock layers, glue them in a specific sequence, and label the relative age of each layer from oldest to youngest.

activities.mastery_criterion: Correctly matches the dark soil to the surface horizon, sandy to subsoil, and gravel to parent material, with valid justifications.
activities.task: Students examine sealed transparent bags containing different safe soil materials (e.g., dark potting soil, sandy subsoil, gravel). They must match each bag to its likely horizon based on visual characteristics and justify their choice in writing.

activities.mastery_criterion: All five percentages are calculated correctly and accurately represented on the bar graph.
activities.task: Given a worksheet with hypothetical volume data for five different soil samples, students calculate the sand percentage for each and create a bar graph comparing the sand content of the samples.

activities.mastery_criterion: The final station design includes only seismometers and gas sensors, rejecting unrelated equipment.
activities.task: Students design a paper layout for a volcanic monitoring station. They are given a budget of hypothetical points and a catalog of sensors (seismometers, gas sniffers, anemometers, telescopes). They must select only the valid volcanic sensors to 'purchase' and place on their map.

activities.mastery_criterion: The writing clearly draws a parallel between roots holding soil together and rebar holding concrete together.
activities.task: Students complete a quick-write activity comparing the structural role of plant roots in soil to the role of steel rebar in concrete, explaining how both provide internal stabilization.

activities.mastery_criterion: Students can instantly recall and state the correct boundary type for the given arrow diagram.
activities.task: Students participate in a rapid flashcard game in pairs. One student shows a card with arrows, and the other must quickly name the boundary type. They tally correct answers.

activities.mastery_criterion: The concept map logically connects the terms, showing that vegetation/roots increase stability and decrease erosion/runoff.
activities.task: Students create a concept map connecting the terms: Vegetation, Roots, Soil Stability, Water Runoff, and Erosion. They must write linking verbs on the arrows between the terms.

activities.mastery_criterion: All 15 diagrams are placed in the correct bins based on their arrows.
activities.task: Students are given a mixed stack of 15 small diagrams showing various plate movements. They must sort them into three labeled bins (Convergent, Divergent, Transform) as quickly and accurately as possible.

activities.mastery_criterion: Students can verbally distinguish that magnitude is about the energy of the event, while intensity is about the observable effects on the surface.
activities.task: Explain the difference between magnitude (energy released) and intensity (surface damage). Demonstrate by dropping a heavy book and a light book onto a tray of sand from the same height (magnitude difference), then dropping the heavy book onto sand vs a hard desk (intensity/surface effect difference).

activities.mastery_criterion: Students can observe and state that the grass tray lost less soil because the roots held the soil in place.
activities.task: Demonstrate erosion by pouring equal amounts of water over two inclined trays: one with bare soil and one covered with a patch of grass. Collect the runoff in clear cups to show the difference in soil loss. Discuss how roots stabilize the soil.

activities.mastery_criterion: Students can verbally repeat the four stages of fossilization in the correct order.
activities.task: Present a storyboard detailing the four stages of fossilization: death, burial by sediments, compaction into rock, and exposure. Discuss each stage using visual aids and emphasize the chronological order.

activities.mastery_criterion: Students can verbally match the flat land to agriculture and the steep land to conservation.
activities.task: Introduce the concept of land use capacity by showing pictures of flat, fertile plains and steep, rocky hillsides. Discuss why the flat land is suited for intensive agriculture and the steep land for forest conservation based on soil aptitude.

activities.mastery_criterion: Students can verbally identify at least one mass extinction and the Cambrian explosion on the timeline.
activities.task: Introduce the geological time scale, highlighting major mass extinctions and the Cambrian explosion. Use a large timeline on the board to point out these events.

activities.mastery_criterion: Students can match the physical movement of the foam blocks to the terms convergent, divergent, and transform.
activities.task: Demonstrate plate movements using foam blocks on a table. Show blocks colliding (convergent), moving apart (divergent), and sliding past each other (transform). Draw corresponding arrows on the board.

activities.mastery_criterion: Students can correctly state that the bottom layer is the oldest and the top layer is the youngest in a physical model.
activities.task: Introduce the principle of superposition by stacking different colored sand and gravel in clear plastic cups. Explain that the bottom layer was deposited first and is the oldest. Students observe the model and practice identifying the oldest and youngest layers.

activities.mastery_criterion: Students can identify the three main layers in the jar model and state one physical characteristic of each.
activities.task: Build a physical soil profile model in a large clear jar using whole cookies (bedrock), crushed cookies (subsoil), and chocolate cereal (organic topsoil). Discuss the physical characteristics of each horizon as it is added.

activities.mastery_criterion: Students can follow the calculation steps and understand that the sand layer's volume relative to the total volume determines its percentage.
activities.task: Demonstrate soil texture by showing a pre-settled jar of soil and water. Point out the distinct layers of sand, silt, and clay. Measure the total height of the soil and the height of the sand layer with a ruler, and calculate the percentage of sand on the board.

activities.mastery_criterion: Students can correctly identify seismic activity and gas emissions as valid monitoring parameters.
activities.task: Introduce the physical and chemical parameters used to monitor volcanoes (seismic activity, gas emissions). Contrast these with unrelated environmental factors (wind speed, lunar phases) using a sorting activity on the board.

activities.mastery_criterion: Correctly calculating density and hydrostatic pressure in 4 out of 5 problems, and accurately explaining Pascal's principle in a short essay.
activities.task: Students complete a written test covering all concepts of fluid statics, including multiple-choice questions, calculations, and short-answer explanations.

activities.mastery_criterion: One point for the model-consistent pressure comparison and one for limiting it to the stated assumptions.
activities.task: A supplied ideal-flow model specifies steady incompressible flow along one horizontal streamline with no pump or dissipative loss. Its legend relates higher speed to lower static pressure. Compare two labelled points and explain why the legend alone is not a universal rule for every real airflow.

activities.mastery_criterion: Conclusions correctly state that higher hydrostatic pressure results in a faster flow rate.
activities.task: Students investigate how the hydrostatic pressure (depth of water in a container) affects the flow rate of water exiting a hole at the bottom.

activities.mastery_criterion: Designs maximize displaced volume, and justifications correctly reference Archimedes' principle.
activities.task: Students design and build a small boat out of aluminum foil that can hold the maximum number of metal washers without sinking. They must calculate the density of their boat before adding washers and justify their design choices based on buoyancy and displaced fluid.

activities.mastery_criterion: Correct calculation of displaced fluid weight and buoyant force in 4 out of 5 problems.
activities.task: Students solve word problems calculating the volume of displaced fluid and the resulting buoyant force for objects of different shapes and sizes.

activities.mastery_criterion: Distinguishes model from measurement and names pressure or force evidence needed for a quantitative claim.
activities.task: Inspect a supplied drone-flow sketch. Distinguish the model arrows from actual pressure or force measurements and explain why the drawing alone cannot quantify lift. Propose one relevant measurement.

activities.mastery_criterion: Correct calculation of buoyant force and accurate prediction of floating or sinking.
activities.task: Students solve a series of word problems calculating the buoyant force on different objects submerged in various fluids, determining if they will float or sink.

activities.mastery_criterion: One point for the model-consistent pressure comparison and one for limiting it to the stated assumptions.
activities.task: A supplied ideal-flow model specifies steady incompressible flow along one horizontal streamline with no pump or dissipative loss. Its legend relates higher speed to lower static pressure. Compare two labelled points and explain why the legend alone is not a universal rule for every real airflow.

activities.mastery_criterion: Correct use of the flow rate formula and appropriate units in all answers.
activities.task: Students analyze different scenarios (e.g., filling a pool, water flowing through a pipe) and calculate the flow rate or the time required to move a specific volume of fluid.

activities.mastery_criterion: Accurate calculation of hydrostatic pressure using the correct formula and units.
activities.task: Students calculate hydrostatic pressure at various depths for different fluids (water, oil, saltwater) using the density and depth variables.

activities.mastery_criterion: Accurate application of Pascal's principle to find the correct output force.
activities.task: Students calculate the force output of various hydraulic press systems given the input force and the areas of the pistons.

activities.mastery_criterion: Correct calculations and logical rankings based on the principles of statics.
activities.task: Students complete a structured problem set calculating densities of various objects, determining which face of a block exerts the most pressure, and ranking containers based on hydrostatic pressure at the bottom. They peer-review their answers using a rubric.

activities.mastery_criterion: Correct categorization and justification based on cohesion or adhesion forces.
